settings.editor: Trusted by patients from Sydney to Narrabri
What you notice
If this sounds like your pain, there is a structural reason for it. The assessment is what finds it.

• Knees that touch while the ankles stay apart
  • Feet that roll inwards, with the arches dropping
  • A knock-kneed look that is worse when tired or running
  • Aching on the inside of the knee, or at the front
  • Tripping, or an awkward running style

As with bow legs, some of this is expected at certain ages and corrects with growth. Where it persists, the knee is usually reflecting what is happening above and below it: an angle at the hip that drops the thigh bone inwards, a foot that rolls in and lets the arch fall, and tight muscles at the front of the hip that tilt the pelvis forward. A leg length difference can produce it on the longer side only.

image.alt: School children sitting on a wall with their legs hanging down

settings.editor: <figcaption>School children sitting on a wall with their legs hanging down</figcaption>
How we diagnose it
Knock Knees is diagnosed with the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment, so treatment is prescribed against a finding rather than a symptom.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
We assess your child standing, walking and running, and measure the angle at the knees against what is expected for their age.
02
We look at the hip, the pelvis and the foot together, and explain which of them the knee is responding to.
03
Where nothing needs doing we say so and set a review. Where it does, the plan is aimed at the level the problem is coming from.

Questions

settings.title: Will my child grow out of it?

settings.editor: Often, yes. A degree of it is normal at certain ages. The assessment tells you whether your child is within the expected range, and whether the feet are adding to it.

settings.title: Is it the same as flat feet?

settings.editor: They travel together. A foot that rolls in and loses its arch lets the knee drop inwards, which is why flat feet and knock knees are often assessed at the same time.
Where it persists, load concentrates on the inner side of the knee and at the front of the kneecap. In adults that is linked with knee pain.
Usually orthotics to support the foot and change how the knee loads, with hands-on work and stretches for the muscles at the front of the hip.

settings.editor: Trusted by patients from Sydney to Narrabri
What it is
Neural therapy uses injection to stimulate a repair response in tissue that is not healing on its own. At Dr. Abbie Clinics it is used alongside prolotherapy.
It is considered for persistent problems where other treatment has not resolved the pain. Whether it is appropriate for you is decided at the assessment.
Where it is available

image.alt: A podiatrist supporting a patient’s foot during treatment

settings.editor: In detail
Our injection therapies include prolotherapy, short for proliferation therapy: an injection that encourages the body to grow new tissue where it has become weak.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient before treatment

settings.editor: The order we follow
Biomechanically
Find the reason the joint or tendon is under strain.
Orthotics and joints
Correct the foundation with orthotics and free up the joints.
Last, not first
Only then inject, so the repaired tissue is not put straight back under the same strain.
01
A dextrose (sugar-water) solution is injected where a ligament or tendon attaches to bone. It causes local inflammation, which increases blood supply and prompts the tissue to repair itself.
02
Ankles, knees and hips: joint wear, weakened ligaments and long-standing tendon problems.
03
It varies with how each person heals. Your practitioner will talk you through what to expect for your condition.
How it works here
Neural Therapy is prescribed against a diagnosis, never against a symptom. That is what the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment is for.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
The assessment establishes the diagnosis and whether injectable therapy is a reasonable step for it.
02
If it is, your podiatrist will explain what is involved, including what to expect afterwards, before anything goes ahead.
03
As with every treatment here, it is paired with addressing the mechanical cause rather than used on its own.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine demonstrating a lower limb assessment, with alignment marked on the leg and practitioners observing

settings.editor: Trusted by patients from Sydney to Narrabri
What you notice
If this sounds like your pain, there is a structural reason for it. The assessment is what finds it.

• A tender lump at the top of the shin bone, just below the kneecap
  • Pain at the front of the knee that is worse with running, jumping and stairs
  • Pain when kneeling
  • Often during a growth spurt, and more often in boys
  • Usually one knee, but it can be both

At this age the top of the shin bone is still growing and is softer than the bone around it. The tendon from the kneecap attaches there. Where the shin is rotated — inwards or outwards — and the hip muscles tighten to compensate, a twist is created through the knee. The tendon then pulls on the growing area repeatedly, which inflames it and can pull it away from the bone, forming the lump. Bone and soft tissue growing at different rates is part of why it happens when it does.

image.alt: Diagram of Osgood-Schlatter disease, showing the patellar tendon pulling on the growth plate at the top of the shin bone

settings.editor: <figcaption>Diagram of Osgood-Schlatter disease, showing the patellar tendon pulling on the growth plate at the top of the shin bone</figcaption>
How we diagnose it
Osgood-Schlatter is diagnosed with the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment, so treatment is prescribed against a finding rather than a symptom.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
We assess the whole limb rather than only the knee, because the twist through the knee usually starts below it or above it.
02
We identify where the rotation is coming from — the shin, the hip, or the way the foot is loading — and explain what we found.
03
Treatment is prescribed against that finding, and staged around your teenager’s growth and sport.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine demonstrating a lower limb assessment, with alignment marked on the leg and practitioners observing

settings.editor: Trusted by patients from Sydney to Narrabri
What you notice
If this sounds like your pain, there is a structural reason for it. The assessment is what finds it.

• Feet that turn outwards when walking or running
  • A waddling appearance to the walk
  • Tiring quickly compared with other children
  • Uneven wear on the outside of the shoes

Like in-toeing, out-toeing can originate at the foot, the shin or the hip. Some is expected at particular ages and resolves with growth. What matters is whether it is within the expected range for your child and whether it is causing symptoms.

image.alt: A young child standing barefoot, showing foot position

settings.editor: <figcaption>A young child standing barefoot, showing foot position</figcaption>
In detail
Out-toeing often comes from the shin bone being twisted outwards, called external tibial torsion. Like pigeon toe, it is often inherited.

image.alt: A dancer on pointe, where turnout should come from the hip

settings.editor: The measurements behind it
13–18° from age 6
Some outward turn is healthy. Well beyond that range, the foot points out from the knee down.
45° each way
Tight groin and hip-flexor muscles show the body is compensating for an outward-turned shin.
0–4°
Checked alongside the shin, because the two affect each other.
01

settings.title: Turnout from the hip, not the foot

settings.editor: In dancers, forcing turnout from the knee or foot, rather than the hip, can lead to knee, groin, lower back and stomach pain over time.
02
An outward-turned shin compensated by tight groin muscles twists the knee. That adds to the pull on the growing area below the kneecap in active teenagers.
03
Stretches, in-toe gait-plate orthotics to guide an outward-turned shin, and re-measuring every few months. See children’s podiatry.
How we diagnose it
Out Toe is diagnosed with the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment, so treatment is prescribed against a finding rather than a symptom.

settings.editor: Trusted by patients from Sydney to Narrabri
What you notice
If this sounds like your pain, there is a structural reason for it. The assessment is what finds it.

• Feet that turn inwards when walking or running
  • Tripping more than other children the same age
  • A twisting appearance from the knee or the hip down
  • Complaints of tired or sore legs after activity

In-toeing can come from the foot, the shin or the hip, and which one it is matters because they behave differently as a child grows. Where the shin bone itself is twisted inwards, the body often hides it by tightening the hip muscles rather than correcting it, so it can look better while the twist is still there.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine examining a child’s feet

settings.editor: <figcaption>Dr Abbie Najjarine examining a child’s feet</figcaption>
In detail
Pigeon toe often comes from the shin bone being twisted inwards, called internal tibial torsion. It is often inherited, passed down from a parent.

image.alt: A young child walking on the sand

settings.editor: The measurements behind it
13–18° from age 6
Measured at the ankle, a healthy shin turns slightly outwards. A negative angle means it turns in.
45° each way
Ideally the hip turns equally in and out. Tight outer hip muscles show the body is compensating.
0–4°
A twisted shin often makes the feet roll in as well.
01

The in-toeing you can see often lessens. But where it comes from the shin, the body usually hides it rather than correcting it: the hip muscles tighten to turn the leg back out. That is why it is worth assessing rather than waiting.
02
With the shin turning in below the knee and the thigh turning out above it, the knee is caught in the middle. In adults this is linked to knee pain.
03
Monitoring as your child grows, stretches for the hip muscles that have tightened to compensate, orthotics where the feet roll in, and regular re-measurement. See children’s podiatry.
How we diagnose it
Pigeon Toe is diagnosed with the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment, so treatment is prescribed against a finding rather than a symptom.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
We assess how your child stands, walks and runs, and compare that against what is expected for their age.
02
We work out which level the rotation is coming from and explain it in plain terms.
03
Where nothing needs doing we will say so and set a review. Where it does, treatment is staged around growth.

What you notice
If this sounds like your pain, there is a structural reason for it. The assessment is what finds it.

• Pain along the arch or where it meets the heel
  • Worst with the first steps of the day
  • Eases with movement, then returns after rest
  • Sore to press along the inside of the arch

Pronation elongates the plantar fascia. As the foot rolls in and the arch drops, the fascia is stretched on every step, and that repeated stretching causes micro-tears at the base of the heel, where it attaches. How much load it takes, and from which direction, depends on foot alignment, a change in activity or footwear, and the way the leg above is working.

image.alt: Diagram of the plantar fascia showing inflammation and tearing

settings.editor: <figcaption>Diagram of the plantar fascia showing inflammation and tearing</figcaption>
In detail
The plantar fascia is a band of tissue running from the heel bone to the ball of the foot. Plantar fasciitis is what happens when it is repeatedly over-stretched at its attachment on the heel.

image.alt: Pain highlighted under the heel where the plantar fascia attaches

settings.editor: How it progresses
Early
Constant, repetitive strain causes tiny tears and inflammation where the fascia attaches to the heel.
Longer term
The body lays down thickening and scar tissue. There is usually no longer inflammation, and it becomes harder to treat.
Compensation
A small bony growth forms at the attachment.
01

When the foot rolls in too far, the arch drops and the foot lengthens. That stretches the fascia at its heel attachment on every step. Overnight it is not under load, which is why getting out of bed hurts most.
02
The fascia has inner, central and outer bands. Inner heel pain is linked with rolling in, outer heel pain with rolling out, and centre heel pain with both.
03
If one leg is longer, that foot may roll in more to level the body up, straining the inner heel. The plan can then include raising the shorter leg, not just supporting the arch.
04
Orthotics and additions, strapping, massage and foot adjustments, shockwave, dry needling and injection therapy.
How we diagnose it
Plantar Fasciitis is diagnosed with the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment, so treatment is prescribed against a finding rather than a symptom.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
We look at how the arch loads when you walk rather than only at rest, because the fascia is loaded as you move.
02
We identify what is increasing that load and explain what we found before anything is prescribed.
03
Treatment is matched to the finding, which is why the plan differs between two people with the same diagnosis.

settings.editor: Questions

settings.title: Do I need a referral to see a podiatrist at Bowral?

settings.editor: No. Podiatry is a primary contact profession in Australia, so you can book directly. If you are on a Medicare care plan your GP will refer you, and we can bill that.

settings.title: Do you make custom orthotics at Bowral?

settings.editor: Orthotics are prescribed here from your assessment and manufactured at our Kirrawee head office. Usually ready within 7 to 10 days.

settings.title: Do you treat children at this clinic?

settings.editor: Yes. Children’s podiatry is available here, including assessment for in-toeing, flat feet and growing pains. Children are seen at all of our clinics.

settings.title: How long is a first appointment?

settings.editor: Allow about 45 minutes. That covers the biomechanical assessment, the diagnosis and an explanation of the treatment plan before anything is prescribed.

settings.title: Can I claim my health fund rebate on the spot?

settings.editor: Yes. Bowral has HICAPS, so private health rebates come off at reception. Medicare care plans and NDIS plans are accepted.
